Why are there still altruists evolutionarily? I hate to say it, but the other answers to this question, even from folks who normally write good stuff, are wrong, misleading, or fudging the definition of altruism. True altruism goes beyond mere cooperation or being helpful. It means being helpful without any benefit to yourself, or from an evolutionary perspective, at least a benefit to your own genes. And natural selection is never going to favor such behaviors of pure altruism. To the extent that altruism does happen and has an evolutionary origin, it's because evolution is a mindless process without perfect aim, and some behaviors are missing their target. To begin with, there's the concept of kin selection. What's really important to evolution is increasing the copies of your genes. When parents help their direct offspring, nobody refers to that as 'altruism', since the offspring share half of the genes from each parent, so it's obvious that the parents are protecting their own genetic legacy. But you share genes with more relatives than just your own children. As the famed biologist JBS Haldane supposedly once quipped, "I would gladly give up my life for two brothers or eight cousins." Promoting your own genes by helping relatives is not altruism, at least in an evolutionary sense. Cooperation beyond relatives can also be favored by natural selection, but that's because cooperation brings benefits to all parties involved, so it's not really altruism, either. This can even cross species boundaries, such as the textbook example of cleaning stations in coral reefs, where cleaner fish and shrimp will pick the dead skin and parasites off of larger fish, even fish that could easily eat them if they tried. The cleaners get a meal, while the cleanees get improved hygiene. Everyone benefits from this cooperation (well, everyone but the parasites). One of the other answers to this question used the example of helping an injured member of your tribe to recover, so that they can once again become productive and contribute to your tribe in the future. Well, that's the ulterior motive right there – their future contributions. Going even further, in complex social groups like we humans form, individuals benefit immensely from being a part of the tribe, but everybody also has a vested interest in keeping out freeloaders and cheats. So public displays of charity help to increase your social capital, showing that you are a valuable, contributing member of the tribe, which will provide you with indirect benefits down the road. So even public displays of charity aren't altruistic in these conditions. (I’m not saying people are so conniving in their motivations, but why evolution would have instilled such instincts in us.) The tribalism that's so common in human societies helps to show that these behaviors really are for the benefit of the individual, and not altruism. From a selfish perspective, it makes sense to help out those in your own tribe, since they're more likely to be family in the first place (kin selection), or folks who will be able to help you out in the future (long term cooperation). People are much, much less charitable to non-relatives, or to those outside their own tribe (the other). But like I said way up in the beginning, evolution doesn't have perfect aim. It's not a conscious creator who implements designs the same way an intelligent designer might. Evolution often results in good enough, not perfection. So a general instinct to help those in your own tribe will be helpful, but could spill over into helping strangers. Parental instincts to help your own children and those of your near relatives can spill over into helping babies in general. And of course, in the more intelligent animals like us apes, dolphins & whales, some birds, and a few others, our extremely complex personalities provide even more opportunities for individuals to consciously choose actions that may not be in their evolutionary best interests. It doesn't mean natural selection favors those choices, but rather that natural selection does favor the larger set of complex behaviors, because their benefits outweigh the occasional 'poor' choice (poor in an evolutionary sense, not necessarily in a moral one). Finding examples of true altruism that weren't just the occasional misfiring of otherwise evolutionarily beneficial behaviors would actually be a major blow to our current understanding of evolution. Outside the somewhat controversial theories of group selection, there's no mechanism to explain why an organism would help out another organism if it didn't gain at least some benefit for itself or its genes. But cooperation, tit-for-tat, kin selection, and complex behaviors in intelligent animals do all go to show that the alternative isn’t a cut-throat, dog eat dog world. There are still plenty of reasons evolution will favor cooperation, since cooperation can bring benefits to everybody.

Have you ever met an intelligent creationist? I've met intelligent creationists, but never any creationists in person who actually understood evolution. Every time I talked to an intelligent creationist about how they thought evolution worked, I invariably found that they didn't actually understand. Their views tend to be a mish-mash of Lamarckism, teleological thinking, evolution being progression towards a goal, and human exceptionalism, along with a lack of knowledge of how evolution works, and even a lack of knowledge of modern day organisms. These types of misconceptions drive such questions as wondering why there are still monkeys if we evolved from monkeys (though it's never why there are still birds if penguins evolved from birds), or wondering whether the first fish to crawl onto land would have had either gills or lungs (totally ignoring all the existing fish that have both). You can browse through the Index to Creationist Claims to get an idea of the types of arguments creationists might use. I don't wholly blame these folks, either. They were raised in an environment where creationism was the default, from their parents to their preachers, to possibly even their school teachers (my daughter's high school biology teacher made an announcement at the start of the lesson on evolution that, as a Christian, she didn't believe in it, herself, but it was just part of the curriculum that they had to get through). They were taught all these misleading creationist arguments from people they trusted from a very young age. So the smartest kids were actually the best at absorbing those lessons. And since it takes a while for people to fully develop critical thinking skills, and a fair amount of discipline to go back and apply that to things you think you already know, it's hardly a surprise that those bright kids brought up within a creationist environment carried that belief into their adulthood. (And to be fair, ask yourself how you know that matter is composed of atoms and that atoms are composed of even smaller particles – do you really understand the evidence, or is it just common knowledge that you were taught back when you were younger?) I will say, though, that the number of intelligent, well-educated creationists I've met is rather small. You can definitely see a correlation vs. education level (note that graph is a bit old from 2005): SOURCE: Americans Weigh In on Evolution vs. Creationism in Schools So yes, I've met otherwise intelligent folks who were also creationists. But once you talk with them, it almost invariably turns out that, for whatever reason, they don't actually understand evolution. I have yet to meet a single person in real life who could accurately explain evolution yet still rejected it.

If a ball is spinning and generating artificial gravity, would the force be on the outer surface or inner surface? A ball is not really a great shape for this. When engineers talk about spinning a spaceship or space station to create artificial gravity, what it really is is centrifugal force. I'm not going to get into a big discussion on centripetal vs. centrifugal force. Just realize that in a rotating reference frame, centrifugal force is a 'useful fiction' to help engineers calculate forces while keeping their coordinate system aligned with the rotating object, and that centripetal force points towards the axis of rotation. ABOVE: Centripetal force is the 'real' force in a non-rotating reference frame. Centrifugal force is the useful fiction from the rock's point of view. SOURCE: Centrifugal Force- Definition, Principle, Examples (vs Centripetal force) For this reason, when engineers propose rotating space ships or space stations to create 'artificial gravity', they tend to follow a few standard forms that make the best use of centrifugal force. The simplest is putting your main crew compartment and some type of counterweight on opposite ends of a tether, and having them spin around their common center of gravity, with the tether holding them together. ABOVE SOURCE: Should we give up on artificial gravity? A common one in sci-fi stories for a bigger ship/station is to make it into a ring, so that you can take advantage of the entire ring for artificial gravity. Here's the classic example from 2001: A Space Odyssey: SOURCE: Sci-fi Gifs And here's kind of what it would be like inside such a station: SOURCE: Quora For the really fanciful sci-fi stories, they might use something know as an O'Neill cylinder. This is a truly gigantic version, where you have a huge cylinder spinning, which can create entire enclosed habitats: ABOVE: I know the labels are in Russian (I can't read them, either), but it's about the best diagram I could find SOURCE: Humanoid History (@HumanoidHistory) on X That said, there are some very significant engineering challenges to doing any of these configurations, such that none of them may be practical, especially in the near term. For any upcoming missions to Mars, for example, the astronauts are probably just going to have to deal with a zero-g journey. So, with all that explanation, I hope the answer to your question is obvious. The artificial gravity will be on the inside surface of your spinning ball, due to the centrifugal force 'pushing' you away from the axis of rotation. If you were on the outside surface, you would be flung away from the ship/station. But you should also see why a ball wouldn't be a great shape for this. Only the 'equator' would have the centrifugal force perpendicular to its surface. Everywhere else would be on a slope, like a hill. The points right at the axis of rotation would be completely vertical from an astronaut's perspective.

Why is there so much debate over the math question 12÷2(2+4) =? A few other answers have said it's because the expression is ambiguous. But that's not really it. The expression isn't ambiguous at all. As an engineer myself, there's only one way to interpret that expression correctly. No. The issue is that lots of folks' exposure to math doesn't go much if at all beyond the high school level, and simplistic understandings of order of operations like PEMDAS or BODMAS. They don't know any further conventions that affect order of operations. The thing that makes this expression completely unambiguous is that there's no symbol in between the 2 and the parenthesis. That makes it clear that 2(2+4) is a single unit that can't be broken up. So the only appropriate way to interpret this expression is: 12 2 ( 2 + 4 ) What might have made this expression a bit ambiguous would have been to add a multiplication symbol: 12÷2×(2+4) Then it could be conceivable to interpret it a bit differently, perhaps instead as: 12 2 ( 2 + 4 ) However, even then, many engineers might interpret it the first way, keeping 2×(2+4) as a single unit as the denominator of the fraction. The reason is that when you're writing math 'inline' as opposed to formatting it the way math should really be written, division symbols are often treated as the fraction bar, with everything to the left assumed to be the numerator, and everything to the right assumed to be the denominator, and not cluttering things up with parentheses. As just one example, here are the definitions of some coefficients from one of my own engineering books, which I can assure you follow the convention that I just described (“my own” is in I own it, not that I wrote it). Really, if you wanted it to be 12/2, you'd probably put the parentheses around that to make it clear that 12/2 was a fraction, and instead write something like: (12/2)(2+4) But just to summarize, the expression as written in the original question isn't ambiguous. The issue is that lots of folks with only limited exposure to math don't know all the conventions affecting order of operations. And if there ever are any questions about ambiguity in an expression you’re writing, don’t be afraid to use parentheses.

Think of a small submarine 10 miles deep in the ocean, 1 gallon of water now drives a generator at 80k PSI, then energy is used to separate hydrogen from water and moved to the surface for use. Any holes in this thought experiment? I don't see any 'holes', per se. It just doesn't seem practical for any real world purposes. If I understand the description in the question, you'll end up with something like this on your sub: You've got a tank big enough to allow 1 gallon of sea water to drive a turbine to generate power, and that power will be used for electrolysis to create hydrogen and oxygen. Pressure can be thought of as energy per volume: So, just rearranging a bit, energy is pressure times volume. You need some type of pressure differential to get any work out of that, which is why the contraption has that tank at atmospheric pressure in the diagram above. But since atmosphere pressure is so much lower than the water pressure that deep, we can just assume it's negligible. Anyway, assuming everything was 100% efficient (which it won't be), using the correct value of 16k psi for the pressure in the deepest part of the ocean, and that I’ve done all my math properly, that 1 gallon of water has a potential energy of 308k ft-lb or 0.156 hp-hr, or in terms more familiar to folks who aren't U.S. based engineers, 418 kJ or 116 Wh. In contrast, a AA battery has roughly 3.9 Wh. So your device, at most, has the potential to generate as much energy as 30 AA batteries. In actuality, after all of the efficiencies are accounted for, it will be even less than that. I think your sub is going to need more than 30 AA batteries worth of energy to complete its mission, so you're spending more energy to perform this mission than what you get out of it. So, while this device could theoretically generate hydrogen in principle, there are far more practical ways of generating power.

I'm not convinced any non-theistic worldview is true because non-theists haven't provided any evidence. I can't make myself believe something without evidence, so can any non-theist please provide evidence that any non-theistic worldview is true? You've got a weird way of approaching this question. Take fairies, for example. As you said, if you "can't make [your]self believe something without evidence", and there's no compelling evidence for the existence of fairies, the default position is to lack belief in fairies, or to take a non-fairiest worldview. If you needed some type of positive evidence for the non-existence of fairies, you'd be stuck in some weird ontological limbo. With no evidence for the existence of fairies, you couldn't believe in fairies, but with no evidence against the existence of fairies, you couldn't believe in their non-existence. But it's not just fairies. This goes for anything. You can build up positive evidence for the existence of something. It's much, much harder to build up evidence for the non-existence of something. That's why the burden of proof has developed the way it has. In general, it's up to the person claiming that something exists to prove their case. The rest of us have no need to take their claims seriously until they have such evidence. To borrow a somewhat silly example from the Internet, do you have any evidence against the existence of Eric The God-Eating Magic Penguin? Wouldn't it seem a bit ridiculous to say that just because you can't find any evidence against Eric, that you're not going to take the non-Ericist position? I hope you see where this is going. If gods exist, the burden of proof is on the people claiming that they exist. Until they can provide compelling evidence, the rest of us are under no obligation to take their claims seriously. Just like with fairies, the lack of evidence makes the default position a non-theistic worldview.

Marriage I remember when our Catholic priest found out my parents had been married in a Lutheran church. He said something to the effect of, 'You mean you're not married?' How is it possible for a specie to pass on evolved genes when it has no power to send genetic messages to its descendants billions of years down the line? I don’t expect anyone to know the answer to this one? You've correctly hit on a major misconception that many people seem to have about evolution – that certain mutations or traits should somehow appear in anticipation of some future adaptation. But as you pointed out, that can't happen. Just take a look at the natural world around us today. Every organism is adapted to its current environment and niche. All organisms throughout history have been the same way. The only mutations that were favored by natural selection were beneficial to those organisms in their own time and place. Where some creationists go off the rails is failing to see how certain adaptations could have been the result of countless intermediate stages. Perhaps the quintessential example is eye evolution. The common creationist argument is something along the lines of eyeballs being exquisitely interconnected systems that wouldn't function without all of their current components in place. As I've seen it put too many times, 'What use is half an eye?' But less complex eyes than our own really are useful and functional. We see them in living animals, from something like a hydra which has only photo-sensitive neurons, to starfish with pigment spots, to snails with pigment cups that can detect direction of light without making an image, to nautiluses with pinhole eyes without a lens, to complex 'camera' eyes like us humans or squids. ABOVE: Evolutionary pathway for camera eyes SOURCE: Visualizing the Evolution of Vision and the Eye ABOVE: And since not all eyes are like ours – Evolutionary pathway for compound eyes SOURCE: Visualizing the Evolution of Vision and the Eye Evolution didn't need to preserve adaptations towards a full camera eye in anticipation of that complex configuration. Every step along the way was a useful adaptation, improving the vision in each of those organisms. I've seen this question asked about plenty of other adaptations as well, from arms and legs, to the lungs of us land animals (many people don't seem to know how many existing fish breathe air), and more. I don't want to make this answer too long, but if you're curious about some of those other traits, here are a few more answers you might want to read: Anyway, I hope this answer helps. You're correct in that natural selection can't favor mutations in anticipation of some far off future benefit. Mutations have to be beneficial to an organism in its immediate surroundings. But over many generations, building incrementally on the benefits of generations past, this has still lead to remarkable adaptations.

Can a truck be engineered to fly by designing the gearing required to extract torque off the motor's axis and using it to move the right sized props? If it had retractable wings, would the engine be powerful enough to keep it in stable flight? Let's take a look at this with some simple back of the envelope math. Google tells me that an 18 wheeler weighs around 35,000 lbs empty, and around 80,000 lbs fully loaded, while they typically have around 500 hp engines. Here's a graph of peak lift to drag ratios (L/D) of various aircraft. Our 18 wheeler with retractable wings isn't going to be anywhere near as streamlined as any of these planes, but just for the sake of argument (remember, this is just a back of the envelope calculation), let's be optimistic and pick an L/D of 20. ABOVE SOURCE: https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Variation-of-L-D-max-for-different-aircrafts_fig8_321107730 So, for the empty truck weighing 35,000 lbs, a L/D of 20 means it will have a drag of 1750 lbs, and hence need to create a thrust matching that. For the fully loaded 80,000 lb truck, that works out to 4000 lbs of drag/thrust. Next, we can just use the super simple fact that you can calculate power based on thrust and velocity as: P=T*V Or, going the other way around: T=P/V Keep in mind, this is ignoring other limitations based on the physical limitations of how propellers work and the resulting losses in real life, predicting impossibly high thrust values at low airspeeds. But it sets an absolute upper limit of thrust possible for a given power. And again, remember – back of the envelope. I already did all the proper unit conversion on a spreadsheet (e.g. hp to ft-lb/s, and mph to ft/s), so here's how that graph of max thrust vs. airspeed works out: So, if you could pull off an L/D of 20 at low airspeeds (which would be a feat in itself), you could conceivably just barely fly a 35,000 lb aircraft with a 500 hp engine, but it'd be pushing it. And you wouldn't be able to go much over 100 mph before you ran out of power. For the fully loaded 80,000 lb truck, forget it. You're simply not going to be able to generate enough thrust with that engine. If I took this analysis a step further, and actually did some simple modeling of propellers, looking at the thrust you could get for a given diameter, it would just get even worse. Momentum theory sets further limitations on propeller thrust even lower than the simple calculation up above. (more info: Theoretical Max Propeller Efficiency) And all this was being super generous, assuming a L/D of 20 for a vehicle as aerodynamically ugly as an 18 wheeler. For something that boxy, without adding a bunch of fairings, you'd be looking at an L/D well under 10. What this really goes to show is that flying takes a lot of power. That's why we only use airplanes when we need to get somewhere in a hurry. If you have the time, ground transportation is much more economical. (And of course, trains are even more economical than trucks, and boats and ships are even more economical, yet.)

Why did Tim Walz put female tampons and pads in the boys washroom? I have to say, this is one of the stranger tempests in a teapot I've seen in a while. The reality seems like such a mundane law (albeit very beneficial) that I’m surprised it’s managed to draw this much attention. But while most of the manufactured controversy came out of the right-wing, some left-wing responses have also been a bit more rationalization after the fact rather than what the law originally intended, and based more around conjecture than what's actually going on in Minnesota (i.e. it didn't have anything to do with logistics). So first – the civics lessons. Tim Walz didn't write this law. He didn't campaign on it or provide a draft for the legislature to act on. The law was originally sponsored by Sandra Feist in the Minnesota House, in a standalone bill, HF 44 , and then got included in the much larger Education Finance Bill, HF 2497. After going through the full process in the Minnesota House and Senate, the Education Finance Bill was eventually approved by majorities in both chambers, and so Tim Walz signed it into law. But this whole initiative of providing menstrual products to student was never something that Walz himself led. The main purpose of the law originally proposed by Feist is to provide menstrual products to students. This isn't some revolutionary idea new to Minnesota. There are similar laws on the books in 28 states and D.C. to address what some describe as "period poverty". According to Period Products in Schools, 1 in 4 students struggle to afford such products. And one study of a program in NYC found a 2.4% increase in attendance when free period products were offered to students. As one of the students who testified in the Minnesota House during a hearing on the legislation put it, "We cannot learn while we are leaking" (source: Minnesota may soon OK free menstrual products in schools. These teens led the way). ABOVE SOURCE: Period Products in Schools - Alliance for Period Supplies If you want to read the law for yourself, go to the full text of HF2497. It's easy to find the relevant portions. Just do a search for 'menstrual'. Here's the main portion: ARTICLE 1 GENERAL EDUCATION Section 1. [121A.212] ACCESS TO MENSTRUAL PRODUCTS. A school district or charter school must provide students with access to menstrual products at no charge. The products must be available to all menstruating students in restrooms regularly used by students in grades 4 to 12 according to a plan developed by the school district. For purposes of this section, "menstrual products" means pads, tampons, or other similar products used in connection with the menstrual cycle. There's another passage specifying that the budget for this will be "$2 times the adjusted pupil units of the school district for the school year", and another passage including these menstrual products in a list of allowed purposes for "Total operating capital revenue". Note that there's no mandate that tampons have to be supplied in the boys restroom. However, the language was gender neutral, allowing for discretion at the local levels for schools to implement this law. And that gender neutral language was on purpose. According to Feist, the sponsor of the original bill: While the vast majority of the period products will be used in the girls’ bathrooms, the decision was made to structure the bill as gender-inclusive in order to ensure that trans and nonbinary students who menstruate would have equal access to the products they need. SOURCE: Yes, Tim Walz signed a law requiring Minnesota public schools to provide free tampons in school bathrooms Also, as noted in the article, Why Republicans are calling Walz 'Tampon Tim' — and why Democrats embrace it, there was opposition to this gender inclusivity when "Some Minnesota Republicans initially tried to limit the initiative to female-assigned and gender-neutral bathrooms, but were unsuccessful." However, it's interesting to note that the Republican who proposed that amendment did go on to support the final bill, as he felt the overall issue was important, and not worth killing over that compromise. It’s also worth pointing out that schools are free to come up with their own plans to implement the law. According to an editorial from the Minnesota based Star Tribune, A reality check on the ‘Tampon Tim’ meme: At Anoka-Hennepin, the state’s largest school district, the free products are not found in traditional male-only bathrooms, a spokesman said. But they are provided for free to all in “nongendered bathrooms,” girls’ bathrooms or from health staffers. I can't say that absolutely no schools in Minnesota have provided tampons in the boys room, but if the largest school district in the state isn't doing so, it's obviously not a requirement of the law, so long as transgender students can still receive menstrual products if they need them. So basically, Tim Walz signed a large law that had a bunch of different sections dealing with multiple aspects of education funding. Among these was a requirement to provide tampons to students for free, which seems utterly reasonable to me. The language was made specifically gender neutral, allowing individual schools to implement the law as they saw fit, so long as they were still complying and supporting all students who needed menstrual products, which also seems pretty reasonable to me. And just to be clear, the law doesn't actually force schools to provide tampons in the boys room, and as proven in practice, at least one school district cited in the news hasn't.

What accidents or incidents have you personally had with deep fryers? Back when I was in high school, I got a job at KFC. There was a certain minimum level for the shortening in the pressure fryers, but they never actually gave us any formal training on proper technique to add more. The method I developed for myself was to cut off a chunk of shortening (it was solid at room temperature), then stab that chunk with the knife, and lower it down into the fryer. That seemed better to me than just throwing the chunk in there and having the hot grease splash. Well, one day, I had a just gotten a big chunk of shortening over the fryer when it fell off of the knife, and sent a huge splash of grease up at my head. I managed to turn to the side and close my eyes, but the grease got half of my face. I immediately went to the sink in the kitchen, and began running cold water over my face. The manager didn't seem to quite know what to do, and couldn't get a hold of my parents, so eventually, somebody gave me a ride home. When I did get home, my parents were out in the yard working (why they never heard the phone – this was a bit before cell phones), and were quite surprised to see me, especially with half my face burnt. So they immediately threw me into the car and drove me to the ER. The ER took me in right away (no waiting around like when you've merely got the sniffles), took me straight to a room, and then promptly treated me with nothing fancier than cold washcloths. Really, that was the only treatment – a basin of ice water with a few washcloths soaking in it, that my mom would swap out when the one on my face started to warm up too much. After a couple hours to draw out as much heat as possible, they sent me on my way with referrals for follow ups. Over the next few days, my face started to look bad. Luckily, it was mostly 'just' second degree burns. But once those blisters started popping and oozing puss all over my face, I was not a pretty sight. One of those referrals was a plastic surgeon, but the only real treatment I needed was bacitracin to prevent infection. All this happened just a couple weeks before graduation. Any open wounds had mostly healed in time, but the skin was still pretty tender, and I was supposed to keep out of the sun. So, I went everywhere with a wide brimmed hat, and avoided sitting out under the sun for all of the graduation rehearsals. I also avoided shaving, so I had that just wrong 17 year old level of stubble – more scruffy than rugged. A couple friends and I had also planned a cross country road trip right after graduation, which meant upgrading our provisional drivers licenses to full licenses, so we wouldn't have any restrictions driving during the trip. Oh man was that a horrible drivers license photo, between the scruff, red face, and completely unkempt hair once I took off the wide brimmed hat. Whenever anybody complained about a bad drivers license photo, I always had them beat (and they always agreed). Thankfully, I only developed a few minor scars, that weren't even that obvious when I was clean shaven, but are now completely hidden by my (adult) beard. Anyway, I was more careful adding shortening after that. I even got workman’s comp out of it.

Who was the first ancestor of ours who walked on four legs? It depends on what you mean by 'walking'. It's also a bit cloudy because of the incompleteness of the fossil record. Let's address the definition of 'walking', first. Take a look at this video of a modern day creature (i.e. not our ancestor, and not even particularly closely related): I think it’s reasonable to say that it's walking along the coral reef, using its fins much like legs. And the truth is, walking underwater is a useful form of locomotion. Handfish and frogfish are also quite well known for walking underwater. And it seems that in our own ancestors, walking underwater came first, before any of them ever tried to crawl up onto a mud bank. I found an article that goes into great detail on the origin of tetrapods, The Fish–Tetrapod Transition: New Fossils and Interpretations. Here's a figure from that article, showing the relationships of species know from fossils, along with the general timeframe of when tetrapods evolved: ABOVE: Stratigraphic table of Late Devonian and Early Carboniferous with cladogram of tetrapodomorphs superimposed to show distribution in time. Broad bars show known range, narrow bars show possible range where exact dating is not available. Based on Ahlberg et al. (2008) SOURCE: The Fish–Tetrapod Transition: New Fossils and Interpretations Note that most of those are side branches, not our direct ancestors, so they're really only giving us a general idea of what our ancestors would have been like, not precise snapshots. Still, the first creatures to walk would have been along those lines. Here's another figure, with less animals, but with pictures of the ones that were included, including diagrams of their forelimbs: SOURCE: The origin of tetrapods - Understanding Evolution So, the first of our ancestors to walk underwater probably would have been something along the lines of Panderichthys. The first of our ancestors to spend an appreciable amount of time walking on land would have been something along the lines of Acanthostega. Though keep in mind the timeframes from the earlier figure, and that Acanthostega was living well after the actual first creatures to become so terrestrial. With recent finds over the past few decades, the current fossil record actually already is a lot more complete than when I was a kid. But there are still plenty of transitional species left to be found. I'm excited for scientists to find them so that I can learn about them.

Could Kamala Harris beat Donald Trump? Yes. And Trump could beat Harris. Presidential elections in the past 30 years have all been relatively close. Roughly half the votes will go to either candidate, plus or minus a few percent that decides who will win (and a few more percent to third party candidates). And of course, that whole process gets filtered through the electoral college, so a candidate doesn't even need a majority of the popular vote to win the election. ABOVE SOURCE: United States presidential election - Wikipedia This year will be no different. Trump will get around half the vote. Harris will get around half the vote. Whoever performs best in the swing states will win the overall election. Sure, you've got plenty of people right now making 'guarantees' about who will win. And given that it's really a binary choice, a lot of those people will inevitably end up picking the eventual winner. But it doesn't mean they actually had any better insight than the rest of us. It means they just got lucky by calling the coin toss. I think we can safely predict, at least, that Robert Kennedy is not going to win. Side note: I don't mean to discount polling as worthless. I think it still is useful and valid as long as you understand it's limitations. It's just that polling can't tell you much when elections are decided by less than the polling margin of error. Another side note: This question is from 2016, but for obvious reasons, it's taken on a new found relevance.

Why is the news about the solar eclipse still in the news two days afterwards? Because it was really damn cool, and many of us who saw it are still looking up follow up stories. And considering that those of us who saw it include several high population areas across North America and big cities close enough for people to make day trips out of it (a few million people total traveled to see the eclipse), that’s a lot of potentially interested people. Getting to personally see a total eclipse really is a pretty rare thing, potentially once in a lifetime. Sure, total eclipses happen every year and a half or so, but the path of totality is relatively narrow, and the Earth is pretty big, so most people aren’t all that close to most total eclipses. Getting a total eclipse that passed right over so many major population centers and so close to so many others is going to drive a lot of interest in those locations. How long did it take for humans to evolve from monkeys? Why are there no living monkeys that have evolved into humans? Although I usually avoid answering the A.I. Quora Prompt Generator (QPG) questions, there are already several other answers to this one that all took a different approach than I would have, so let me add my 2¢. Trying to pin specific numbers to this answer comes down to what you want to call a monkey, and whether you think monkeys should be monophyletic, paraphyletic, or polyphyletic. It doesn't change the actual evolutionary history of humans, just the semantics of what's a monkey and what isn't. Here's a diagram to help understand those terms: ABOVE SOURCE: Monophyletic, Polyphyletic, & Paraphyletc Taxa Here are the written definitions from that page: ...a monophyletic taxon is defined as one that includes the most recent common ancestor of a group of organisms, and all of its descendents [as in (a)]. ...a paraphyletic taxon [is] one that includes the most recent common ancestor, but not all of its descendents [as in (c)]. A polyphyletic taxon is defined as one that does not include the common ancestor of all members of the taxon [as in (b)]. Now, here's a broad evolutionary history of primates: ABOVE SOURCE: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0960982212008068 So, the semantic question comes down to, what on that diagram is a monkey? If it's only the New World monkeys and Old World monkeys but not the 'Early simians', then monkeys are a polyphyletic group. That would mean we humans evolved from simians, but not monkeys, so the QPG's question can't be answered. If you think those early simians are themselves monkeys, but want to split apes off into something separate, then monkeys would be a paraphyletic group. Our lineage, the apes, would have split off from the monkeys around 36 million years ago, which would make the answer to the QPG's question 36 million years. But if you think monkeys should be a monophyletic group, then everything descended from those early simians should be counted as monkeys. And then the question is back to being unanswerable, since we humans would still be monkeys, ourselves. My most recent monkey ancestors would be my mom and dad. I personally descended from monkeys in the late 1970s. That last point does address the QPG's last question. The living monkeys that evolved into humans are us. And the reason why no other monkeys or apes are evolving to be more like us now is because of the Competitive exclusion principle. We humans already occupy the niche of being hyper social technological primates. So other primates need to specialize in other niches that don't compete with ours. Anyway, while the question did come from the QPG, I have seen real people sincerely ask similar questions, so I think this was worth answering. Will drinking beer while still on a calorie deficit affect my fat loss? As the old saying goes – everything in moderation. If you don't drink in moderation, it can be a real whammy to weight loss. First you get all the calories from the beer itself. Beer can range anywhere from around 100 calories for an American light lager to over 300 calories for a Belgian triple. Drink a bunch of craft beers and IPAs for a night on the town with friends, and that could add up to a few thousand calories worth of beer alone. Then, you get the munchies that come along with that, combined with the lower inhibitions caused by the alcohol, and that 3 am trip to the drive thru (with your DD driving, of course) to pick up a double bacon cheeseburger with a large fries sounds like just the thing. Then you've got the hangover the next day, with yet more cravings for greasy fried foods, just adding to the calories. In short, aside from any of the other reasons to avoid overdoing it with beer, you definitely don't want to do so if you're trying to lose weight. But if you do stick to moderation, you should be fine. The key to losing weight is to consume less calories than you expend, and you don't need to stick to diet food to achieve that goal. I myself lost around 60 lbs by eating a normal balanced diet, just less of it. And yes, I still treated myself to occasional desserts and sweets, and usually a few beers over the weekend. Complete abstinence just leads to temptation.

Isn't it crazy that 1 man managed to convince billions of people that they evolved from an animal? Actually, yes it is. That's why Darwin is held in such high esteem as the genius he was, and why he was granted the honor of being buried in Westminster Abbey. Other naturalists had proposed ideas of transubstantiation before Charles Darwin, including his grandfather Erasmus Darwin. However, none of those predecessors had managed to convince the larger scientific establishment to take evolution particularly seriously. And Edward Blyth had hit on ideas of natural selection before Darwin published the Origin, though Blyth's comments on the matter went largely unnoticed. Somewhat famously (at least among us nerds), William Wallace also discovered natural selection independently, and even submitted a joint presentation of papers with Darwin to the Linnaean Society of London in 1858. But this submission also didn't have much impact. What did have tremendous impact was when Darwin finally published his book, On the Origin of Species, in 1859. The arguments and evidence he compiled in that book were enormously compelling. Practically overnight, evolution and universal common descent went from a somewhat disreputable position among fringe academics to accepted mainstream science. It was a monumental work on par with the likes of Newton and Einstein. Much of science progresses by incremental contributions from many different researchers. The subsequent history of evolutionary science after Darwin does follow this more general pattern. Looking through the Wikipedia article on the Modern synthesis, you find plenty of contributors like Ernst Mayr, G. Ledyard Stebbins, Theodosius Dobzhansky, E. B. Ford, Bernhard Rensch, Ivan Schmalhausen, George Gaylord Simpson, R. A. Fisher, William Bateson, Julian Huxley, J.B.S. Haldane, and more. But none of those folks, as intelligent as they were, had the same paradigm shifting impact as Charles Darwin. To put it another way, human knowledge had finally progressed to the point where discovering evolution was practically inevitable. It would have happened eventually. But without Darwin, it would have been a more prolonged process that would have taken a bit longer, and the folks who contributed would probably still be mentioned in the history books, but they wouldn't be household names (just look to Alfred Wegener and continental drift). Darwin was a true genius, with a monumental impact on biology. So yes, it is always a bit crazy when you come across such singular geniuses.

If you are an atheist, how do you explain conscience to yourself? As for YOU, where does it come from? Our innate morality is an evolved instinct as a social animal. Depending on the conditions and the niche, social groups can offer animals synergistic benefits greater than the sum of the individuals. So, you see various levels of social cooperation in all types of packs, herds, tribes, troops, pods, etc., with ants and bees being some of the most extreme examples. Individuals living in such social environments need social instincts, not just to make the group successful, but, and this is the really important part in regards to evolution, so that they're accepted into the group so that they can take advantage of the group benefits for themselves. If you ever watched the show Meerkat Manor, you may recall that meerkats kicked out of the group had much, much worse chances of survival than meerkats living in the group, so there's a very strong selection pressure for meerkats to have instincts that keep them in the group with all the benefits that provides. But it’s not a hippie dippie love fest. There are also conflicting instincts to not be too selfless to the group, lest an individual sacrifice their own reproductive success. Conversely, all members of the group have an interest in identifying and punishing freeloaders and cheats, since they would drag down the success of the group as a whole. Along those same lines, individuals will have an interest in not doing things that would mark themselves as cheats, themselves, to avoid punishment. So, social animals evolve a whole range of complex and sometimes conflicting impulses to maximize their success in such settings. Even actions that go against their own short term self interest may be important in maintaining their long term acceptance within the group. Of course, most of us aren't so Machiavellian and calculating in our own behavior and internal thought processes, but, anthropomorphizing what is in fact a mindless process, natural selection was when it instilled those instincts in us. And so that brings us to where we are today. Perhaps it's easiest to understand the impulses towards selfishness and nepotism for the more direct benefits they would seem to bring us and our offspring. But empathy and conscience are just as important for social animals, since they're critical to our acceptance into social groups and the benefits we get from living in those groups. Note: This answer was adapted from a previous answer: I'll also note, that in the interests of brevity, I didn't even get into topics like kin selection, which add another layer of reasons to cooperate and have feelings of empathy.

I totally believe the evolution theory because it has tons of scientific evidence, but I don't get it how marine life evolved to have lungs, limbs, developed, and somehow intelligent brain to live on land? I think part of the problem is people only think about a stereotypical, generic fish, and don't know about or don't think about the wide variety we see in living fish. You mentioned lungs and limbs, so let's take a look at those. And let's start with the limbs, since it makes for cooler videos. First, here's a frogfish. To be clear, frogfish aren't particularly closely related to the first tetrapods. They're adapted to a fully aquatic lifestyle without ever venturing onto land. But yet, they walk underwater, because it's a better way for them to get around, and especially to use their fins to sit on the ocean floor waiting to ambush prey. And here's a type of walking shark. Again, these are fully aquatic sharks. Their walking isn't some type of planning ahead for a life on the land, but a very useful means of locomotion to prowl around a reef. Next, let's move on to lungs. Air breathing is in fact quite common in many lineages of fish. Oxygen is much more consistent in the atmosphere than in the water, so many fish will surface to swallow gulps of air. Somewhere around 400 million years ago, the common ancestor of bony fish evolved a primitive lung as an outgrowth of the stomach as a way to improve oxygen absorption from these swallowed gulps. Over time, some lineages developed more advanced lungs, while others actually went in a different direction, and the lung evolved into a swim bladder. It just so happens that the lineage that evolved a swim bladder has gone on to become the most successful lineage of fish, so it somewhat biases our perception of what's normal. But a look at the bony fish family tree shows lungs to be rather widespread: ABOVE: The lineages in solid black still have lungs, while the lineages with the dashed outlines evolved swim bladders. SOURCE: How did fish evolve the ability to breathe on land? But even in the lineages that traded lungs for swim bladders, in certain environments, it's still beneficial for fish to be able to breathe air, and so various lineages have evolved new adaptations to allow this. Some fish, like bettas, are so dependent on atmospheric oxygen that they'll 'drown' if they can't get to the surface to take a breath. ABOVE SOURCE: Accessory Respiratory Organs of Fishes (With Diagram) | Chordata | Zoology So, just looking at living species of fish, walking and breathing air are relatively common. And from there, it's not a big step (get it?) to begin spending some time on land. Even that is common enough in living fish, from mudskippers to walking catfish to another species of walking shark that I didn't show here (Epaulette Shark Walks on Land). And once you have fish spending some time on land, well, it's not hard to see how they could become even more specialized to spend even more time on land. In other words, there's no need to ponder any special or unique conditions for why our ancestors would have evolved legs or lungs to make the transition from water to land, since we see plenty of analogs in fish alive right now. They’re simply useful features for some fish to have.

Can an astronaut break the orbit if he jumps from the ISS by pushing himself towards the earth? The gravity will keep increasing. Can he reach earth's surface without burning if he uses a bit of air friction from a device? I'm not sure you really understand the magnitudes involved here. Objects in orbit aren't serenely floating in zero gravity. They're still very much under the influence of Earth's gravity, and constantly in a state of free fall. The only reason they don't hit the Earth is because they're moving so damn fast horizontally: ABOVE: An updated figure of Newton’s original explanation of orbits SOURCE: newton-cannon-orbital-types-Seeds The ISS is orbiting at 17,500 mph. It travels around the entire Earth every 90 minutes. A person can't come anywhere close to generating those speeds by shear muscle power. I saw a few physics forums that estimated that a person could jump somewhere around 5 m/s in zero g. Converting that to my antiquated American units, that's 11.2 mph. So, by jumping perpendicularly to the ISS’s path, you're changing your trajectory by an angle calculated by arcsin(11.2 mph / 17,500 mph), which works out to 0.037°. ABOVE: That change in velocity vector drawn to scale – solid black is the original vector, dashed orange is the new one. That’s not going to change your orbital path much at all. I mean, sure, that's enough to make your orbit slightly different than the ISS, but otherwise it would hardly be noticeable. If the ISS orbit were perfectly circular (which I doubt it is), this 11.2 mph difference would make your new orbit just ever so slightly elliptical, certainly too small of a difference to notice by eye. Basically, when you're already careening around the planet at 17,500 mph, the tiny difference in velocity from human muscle power is only going to have a negligible effect on your path.

If you believe the Bible is fiction, then why would anyone want to write such a work? It's not fiction in the same sense as a novel, where one person sat down to write a story. Much of what ended up in the Bible were legends and stories that had been floating around in that culture for generations, spread largely by word of mouth and oral history. Sure, every once in a while some scribe might have written down a particular version of one of the legends, but these wouldn't have initially taken on the authority of 'scripture', and the legends would continue to develop within the larger society. As a more modern day example, consider Grimm's Fairy Tales. The Brothers Grimm didn't invent these stories themselves. They went around collecting stories from German folklore. You can see this in the books now referred to as the Pentateuch (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy). By using critical analysis to study these books, it's clear that they were the result of combining four prior traditions, now known as the Yahwist, Elohist, Priestly, and Deuteronomist sources, with a round of editing by a person or group known as the Redactor. As just one example from the Old Testament, the Noah's Ark story can trace its origins back to older Sumerian flood myths such as Gilgamesh and Atrahasis. And even the story within Genesis is an intertwining of the Priestly and Yahwist traditions, with conflicting details throughout the story, such as the number of animals to take aboard (one pair of each kind vs. seven pairs of the clean kinds), how long the flood lasted (40 days in the Yahwist source per Genesis 7:17 vs. 150 days in the Priestly source per Genesis 7:24), and twice repeating that Noah went into the ark (7:7-9 and again at 7:13-16). The New Testament development was a bit more rapid, but it was still the result of stories being passed along by word of mouth for decades before a few educated converts to Christianity decided to write them down. Some of those accounts eventually acquired enough of a reputation to be included in the official canon, but many more never acquired the status of 'scriptures', and are regarded as merely early Christian writing. Basically, it's the same as many other mythologies. Nobody necessarily sits down with the intent to create a story from scratch. It's stories that get passed on orally from generation to generation, that develop and morph over the years. Some scribes write down the stories from time to time, and the written versions that strike a chord become canonical.

Some people say Jesus didn’t resurrect but was resuscitated by Joseph of Arimathea, after which he lived secretly in other parts of the world till the age of eighty. If true, why didn’t the apostles know about this and allegedly died as martyrs? I've seen a few of these ideas with a mix of skepticism and credulity, where they're skeptical of the divinity of Jesus and the supernatural aspects of the stories, but they still treat the overall accounting of events as a fairly reliable narrative. Other similar ideas I've heard include Jesus only being in a coma, or disciples secretly stealing the body. But why? If we already think that the gospels are unreliable accounts, then why accept anything in them at face value that needs any more explanation than simply saying it was made up? Now, I don't necessarily mean that all of the stories were intentional lies (though I'm not ruling it out, either). But rather, the gospels weren't written down until decades after the supposed events had taken place, by people who never met Jesus in person and were relying on oral history that had plenty of time to morph and become exaggerated in the retellings. Any stories in the gospels are just as likely (if not more so) to be urban legends or mythologizing than anything based in fact. So, assuming that there was a real Jesus at the core of this legend, and that he was indeed executed by the Roman authorities, how do we explain what happened to his body? More than likely, it was left up on the cross for a while as an example. And whenever it was taken down, it was probably thrown into a mass grave with other executed criminals and political dissidents. Whatever the inspiration for the belief in the resurrection (and I cover some possible scenarios here - Jeff Lewis's answer to What does a Quoran atheist, with a Christian upbringing, think actually happened following Jesus Christ's crucifixion?), there's little reason to trust most of the details in the gospels, and thus little reason to try to think up more rational explanations. There may well never even have been a Joseph of Arimathea in the first place. As far as apostles and/or disciples dying as martyrs, those stories are partly in the same category. The stories in the New Testament of Christian martyrs are themselves of dubious accuracy, so we really don't know just how widespread martyrdom was. And as far as it did happen, well, people believing in urban legends and conspiracy theories is hardly surprising. You can find plenty of modern day examples in just a few minutes on Facebook – even folks so committed to their beliefs that they staged an attempted coup on the U.S. Capitol, and one man who even martyred himself when he lit himself on fire in protest of a criminal trial against former president Donald Trump. People within echo chambers and cults can build themselves up to committing extreme actions that those of us on the outside find shocking and irrational. In short, there's no reason to spend undue effort trying to rationalize all the different details in the gospel stories, when perhaps the most likely explanation of most stories is urban legends and mythologizing that grew over the decades the stories spread as oral history. But just like in the modern day, there were at least some people who did very much believe in those urban legends, probably enough to lose their lives over those beliefs.

Why can't English rugby be as popular as American football in the USA? Well, they started off from the same roots, but then developed along independent paths in their respective countries. So it's no wonder that the version that developed in the USA is more popular in the USA. Both rugby and gridiron football, along with the various other types of football, grew out of a family of British games known as mob football, with different 'house rules' among every group in every town and village that played it. Since it was British colonists who were the first Europeans to come to what would become the U.S. and Canada, they brought along their British sports, including mob football. Round about the mid 1800s, social conditions were finally ripe to begin formalizing these diverse rules with different governing bodies. At the time, the Rugby School's rules were very similar to the rules at several American and Canadian colleges like Harvard, McGill, and Yale (in contrast to the association football rules of Cambridge and the Sheffield Football Club). The New World teams went on to develop new innovations that moved the sport further away from its cousin, rugby, including the line of scrimmage, a system of downs, and then in 1906 the forward pass (Walter Camp was especially influential in many of these innovations). ABOVE: An 1895 football game between Auburn and Georgia looking a lot more like rugby than modern day gridiron football SOURCE: College football - Wikipedia ABOVE: Another pre-forward pass college football game – the University of Minnesota vs. the University of Michigan in 1902 SOURCE: College football - Wikipedia So basically, the two sports started off largely the same, but then went down separate paths in each country. So of course the rules that developed in the USA are more popular here. If most Americans had wanted to play a game more similar to rugby, they wouldn't have changed the rules in the first place.

If everyone around the world rides bicycles that generate electricity and store electricity, how much of humanity's electricity consumption can be offset? The short answer is not much. The long answer is complicated, depending on exactly what you mean by bicycles and how much freedom you'll allow in interpreting the question. The first thing to note, that many people don't seem to realize, is that pedaling to power a generator gets harder and harder the more electrical power you have to provide. They just see the wires, and seem to think that it's no harder than pedaling a free-wheeling bike. But once you try to actually create current with those wires, they create magnetic fields. And those magnetic fields make it more difficult to turn the generator. The more power, the stronger the magnetic field, and the harder it is to pedal. It all goes back to the conservation of energy, and the fact that you can't get something for nothing. Moving on, if you mean stationary cycles, where instead of moving, you're just driving a generator, then you're not going to get much energy at all. Loring Chien already went through the math in his answer. Even taking it to the extreme of people riding such machines for 12 hours a day every day, you only get 10% of the world's electric consumption (the average person can only maintain around 50 - 100 W continuously). And of course, that extreme scenario is not at all practical. You can't do your real job when riding a stationary bike. So if you cut people’s time down to a somewhat more realistic 1 hr per day to leave them time to do other things, then you’re looking at less than 1% of the world’s electric consumption. But even that’s over-estimating the net results. If people are going to perform that much physical exercise daily, their calorie requirements are going to go up. That means more food needs to be grown, stored, and transported, and all of that takes energy. How much of that energy comes from electricity vs. petroleum based fuel is dependent on how quickly EVs displace IC engines, but it’s certainly going to be something (and non-negligible when you’re talking about changes to diet on the scale of the entire world’s population). If you meant adding a generator to regular bikes that generated electricity during the course of normal riding, the numbers come out even lower. Recalling that you can’t get something for nothing, a generator that’s driven through a direct mechanical connection is going to feel like riding the brakes, with the braking force being higher the more power you try to generate. Alternatively, a wind powered generator is going to increase your drag, again forcing you to have to pedal harder. Basically, since you need power to propel the bike, you have to settle for only a fraction of the power that the person can generate going to the generator. That’s why existing generators on bikes are only used for very lower power applications like lights. In short, you’ll generate well, well short of even the 1% from the previous scenario. What about the power savings if everybody rode bikes instead of driving in cars? Now, you’re looking at a double impact, because bikes are much smaller than cars and so don’t require as much power. i.e. The benefit is not just in using human power, but in not needing as much power to begin with. Of course, if you’re just looking at electricity, this is going to be a bigger effect as EVs become more common. What makes this complicated to analyze is that cycling can only replace some uses of automobiles, not all of them, so you have to take that into account. Here’s one study, Ditching the car for walking or biking just one day a week cuts carbon footprint,. If we take CO2 as a proxy for energy consumption, that study found “If just 10% of the population were to change travel behaviour, the emissions savings would be around 4% of lifecycle CO2 emissions from all car travel.” Based on a couple other sources (the Energy Information Administration and the Bureau of Tranpsportation Statistics), transportation in total makes up 37% of U.S. energy consumption, while light-duty short wheelbase vehicles (i.e. cars) makes up 40.3% of that, or around 15% of the total energy consumption. So a 4% savings on automobiles is around a half percent total energy savings. But if you upped that “10% of the population” to “100% of the population”, and it scaled linearly to a 40% savings on car travel, you’d end up with a 6% savings in total energy consumption. That’s not exactly huge, but it’s not negligible, either. To sum up, none of the scenarios result in huge energy savings. Loring Chien’s calculation of people riding all day, every day, still only results in 10% of the world’s electricity requirements. Reducing people’s time on the bikes to 1 hr a day drops that to less than 1%. Putting generators on existing bikes for transportation generates an even smaller percentage than that. The most realistic and achievable scenario is to get people to ride their bikes instead of driving their cars for trips where it’s feasible. Depending on how many people you can get to do this, you’re looking at around 0.5% total energy savings in a more feasible scenario, or 6% in an overly optimistic scenario. But a few percent here and a few percent there can eventually add up to significant savings.

If Christianity is wrong, then why do people believe in it? Before getting into the why, let's get a little perspective. Here is the breakdown of global religious affiliation: SOURCE: The Changing Global Religious Landscape That's a lot of diversity of religions, and none of them are believed by a majority of the world's population. And since many of these religions are mutually contradictory, it stands to reason that most of them are wrong. So, your question isn't just applicable to Christianity. It's applicable to all religions. Why do people believe them, when logically, most of them must be wrong? A big reason is the cognitive bias that Deborah Kelemen has coined 'promiscuous teleology', which is a tendency to see purpose and intention even when it's not really there. Here's an explanation from one paper on the topic, Teleology and the intentions of supernatural agents: Given that according to PT [promiscuous teleology], teleological reasoning develops from an early understanding of intentionality which is then overextended (Kelemen, 1999a), the notion of agency is central to teleology. This is because the only things capable of having intentions are things with minds, and the only things with minds are agents. In this view, just as “chairs are for sitting on” is true only if an agent intends the chair to serve this function, the statement “clouds rain so that plants can grow” is based in the misbelief that plants growing is the intended function of the cloud raining. The difference between these two teleological explanations is that whereas the former implies the intentions of a natural agent (a human), the latter seems to imply the intentions of a supernatural agent. And here's the abstract from a different paper, Promiscuous Teleology: From Childhood Through Adulthood and from West to East: From infancy we continually try to make sense of what goes on around us. One strategy in making sense of things is to look for how things might be purposeful or designed. So useful is this strategy that sometimes it gets overused—what Deborah Keleman calls promiscuous teleology . This chapter reviews research with children and adults across cultures—including recent work in China —that demonstrates that promiscuous teleology is a conceptual default that all peoples share but that may be tamped down through enculturation. Kelemen argues that this teleological reasoning makes certain religious ideas about supernatural agents’ activity in creating or ordering the world largely intuitive. Or to summarize all that, our tendency to see agency everywhere makes us prone to supernatural explanations. Now, there are further questions as to why we might have evolved this cognitive bias in the first place. As I noted in another answer, "There are various explanations for why we might have evolved this bias – from being social animals and having to understand intentions of our fellow humans, to being prodigious tool makers and having an instinctual sense of 'function' for items. And there's no reason the explanations need to be mutually exclusive. (And even all that is assuming it's an adaptive trait, and not just a spandrel of San Marco.)" Add in how children credulously accept lessons from their parents (and understandably so – there's too much knowledge to pass down any other way), and culture, and how these stories morph and change over the generations, and you've got the perfect recipe for a large diversity of supernatural stories to explain various aspects of our world. Christianity just happens to be one of these myths among many.

Will America ever eventually switch to the metric system of measurement for all applications? Eh. Maybe eventually. It seems like we're already slowly transitioning that way. There are certain measurements where metric has been used in the U.S. pretty much my whole life – the sciences (especially at universities), electrical power, measuring volumes of beverages (750 ml, 2 liter bottles, etc.). And there are some where I've seen the switch in my lifetime – particularly U.S. automakers – I only need my 'standard' sockets for classic cars, these days. But there are plenty of areas of society that haven't made the switch, and some of those seem like there's a lot of momentum resisting any change. My own field of aerospace engineering is one. With the high levels of regulation involved, including in the supply chains and standardized hardware, it's not easy for any single company to make the jump to metric on their own. Construction seems like another that will be hard to switch, especially since you still have to support maintenance on existing buildings. We're going to need 2x4s, 3/4" water supply lines, and 4"x10" air vents for a while. In fact, talking to a German friend of mine, even Germany still uses inch based measurements for plumbing for backwards compatibility. But I suspect that the U.S. will probably get there eventually, even if it takes a while. Americans are comfortable enough with metric in our lives where it does exist, so there's little incentive to switch those measurements back to USCS. And there is at least some incentive for international commerce and compatibility to switch to metric in the holdouts. In other words, I only see future changes going in one direction – from USCS to metric. So, like I said, it may take a while, but I suspect the eventual end state is complete metrification (or, at least as complete as European countries are today*). *In addition to my friend's comment about Germany using inches for plumbing, there are plenty of not actual metric units that get used in otherwise metric countries, especially when time is involved in those units – things like km/hr (instead of m/s) or kWh (instead of Joules).

Having a new species require at least 2 mutated species (male and female) with same characteristics, and they need to be around the same area to have any chance of mating. If it is that difficult, how are there so many species on earth today? What you're referring to is saltationism (from the Latin term for jump), sometimes referred to a little more colorfully as the hopeful monster hypothesis. The idea was that large macromutations create new species in a single blow. But, as the colorful name and your question point out, how would such hopeful monsters find partners to mate with? This idea did have some proponents back in the late 1800s and early 1900s, but the incorporation of genetics into evolutionary theory and the Modern Synthesis caused the idea to be mostly abandoned, at least for sexually reproducing animals. Evolution is a gradual accumulation of genetic changes within an entire population. Populations already have genetic diversity. It's why no two individuals look exactly alike. And genetic mutation is decently common. In us humans, for example, it seems that pretty much everybody has a handful of new mutations*. But this genetic diversity doesn't keep us (or other populations of animals) from mating. And the new mutations that do creep into the population don't instantly create new species. They just add to the existing genetic diversity. For a population to split into two species takes time and isolation. The population somehow gets split into two separate populations, let's say Population A and Population B, that can't or don't mate with each other. These constant mutations will continue to spontaneously arise in each population, but they'll be limited to their respective populations. Mutations that arise in Population A, for example, can mix into that population over generations as all those animals mate with each other, but as long as Population B remains isolated from Population A, those mutations won't jump over to Population B. They'll be limited to Population A. And the same goes vice versa for new mutations that arise in Population B. Over time, as each of these population acquires more and more different mutations, they'll become more and more distinct from each other. Eventually, they'll have become different enough to be new species, but it's still a gradual process, with no stark dividing line. ABOVE SOURCE: Islands of speciation and speciation on islands This also explains why species is such a fuzzy boundary, with 'lumpers' and 'splitters' often disagreeing on whether different populations should be separate species, or merely subspecies. For example, a single study from 2020 , showed that there could be anywhere from 2 to 6 different species of giraffe depending on which specific criteria you used to define species. But sexually reproducing animals aren't the only organisms out there. Many types of animals are hermaphrodites, with male and female reproductive organs on the same individual. Many plants also produce male and female reproductive organs (stamens and pistils) on the same plant. If one of these types of organisms were to experience a substantial mutation, then it could potentially create a new species with that individual. In fact, this actually has been observed decently often for plants (take a look at section 5.1 of this page, Observed Instances of Speciation). Another exception is animals that reproduce by parthenogenesis, which is just a fancy term to describe animals where an egg can develop without being fertilized by a male. A notable recent case is the marbled crayfish. Their ancestral species is the slough crayfish from Georgia and Florida. People captured slough crayfish for pets, which led to captive breeding to supply the pet trade. Some time around the mid '90s, somebody in Germany discovered the new species, marbled crayfish, which can reproduce parthenogenetically. This new species like arose from a mutation in a single individual. (You might also see these animals referred to by their German name, marmokrebs.) So, your intuition was partially right about sexually reproducing animals. Even if there were massive mutations that would create a new species in a single individual, the odds of such mutations happening simultaneously to create a male and female of that new species are so astronomically low as to be effectively impossible. But, that’s not the way speciation actually occurs in sexually reproducing animals. It’s a gradual process among populations due the accumulation of many, many mutations. But among other types of organisms that can reproduce by themselves and so don’t have the problem of being hopeful monsters, then speciation can sometimes happen in a single individual. * The overall mutation rate is on the order of 100 - 200 mutations per person. But given that something like 90% of our genome is junk DNA, most of those mutations don't do much at all. Still, it seems that we do all get at least a handful of mutations to functional DNA. When and how were you first introduced to the concepts of intelligent design and creationism? What was your initial reaction to these ideas? I actually can pinpoint this, because I was (thankfully) raised in a reasonably well educated and scientifically literate family, while going to a mainstream Catholic church that didn't really discuss issues of basic science, so evolution was just taken for granted for pretty much all of my childhood. If you want to put it in a less positive light, you might say I was a bit sheltered. My very first inkling that there were such people came in my high school biology class. We were getting ready to start the unit on evolution, when the kid sitting next to me leaned over to ask if I actually believed in evolution. I was taken a bit off guard. That's kind of like asking if you actually believe the world is a globe. But of course, I answered yes. He responded that he didn't, because there were "too many holes" (and yes, I still remember those exact words, because it really was surprising for me at the time to hear someone doubt accepted mainstream science). Anyway, we didn't really discuss it again after that. I just assumed he hadn't watched as many nature documentaries as I had, and that after everything we learned in class and how obvious evolution seemed, surely all his 'holes' must have been filled in. Fast forward several more years to my first job out of college. This was a white collar office job full of other college educated professionals. Around the water cooler one day, one guy mentioned that he thought the Earth was only a few thousand years old. A few of us started laughing thinking that he was joking, because we'd never heard anybody say anything that outlandish about the age of the Earth before. But no, he informed us. He was quite sincere, and there were actually a lot of other folks who believed the same thing he did. He told us to go look up "young Earth" on the Internet (this was back in the early 2000s, so Internet was a thing by then, if not quite as mature as today). So during my lunch break that day, I did. And I was quite surprised at the extent of information I found about Young Earth Creationism. But I still didn't dig too deep, just yet. I thought of the belief as a bit eccentric, kind of like folks who believed they could invent perpetual motion machines, but I didn't comprehend just how widespread it was. Less than a year later, I moved down to a small town in Texas for a new job. As you might expect, creationism was quite a bit more prominent there than inside the D.C. beltway. This was also around the time that Intelligent Design was hitting its peak popularity, with the landmark Kitzmiller decision set to take place in 2005. That's when I really began to pay attention and look into the statistics. And I must say, I really was shocked that nearly half of Americans rejected evolution in favor of creationism. ABOVE: A slim majority of Americans accept evolution (33% + 22%), and the numbers are slowly improving, but the number who reject evolution is still shockingly high SOURCE: Evolution, Creationism, Intelligent Design So, my first minor introductions to creationism came in my high school biology class, and then water cooler talk at my first real job, but it was the move to Texas coinciding with the rising popularity of Intelligent Design that truly got me caught up in the evolution vs. creationism culture wars. And given the religious side of the debate, it also prompted me to dig deeper into my own religious beliefs, which is actually one of the early factors that set me on the path to atheism (though certainly not the only one). Anyway, I really do find evolution quite fascinating, and I'm not sure I would have delved into it quite as deeply if not for the religious controversy. So I suppose that in a way, I have creationists to thank for motivating me to learn as much about evolution as I have (and further, for helping to nudge me towards atheism, which as I’ve said before here on Quora, I find much more fulfilling than Christianity).
