Why did some monkeys stop evolving when other monkeys evolved to be humans? The general trend of evolution is diversification. You start off with one ancestor species. It somehow splits into two populations, who go their own ways and develop into two different species. Those two new species split themselves, becoming more species. For the lineages that survive and don't go extinct, this splitting just goes on and on and on. You can see this in something like the dinosaur family tree. I never hear anybody ask why other dinosaurs didn't all evolve to become triceratops. It actually seems odd to even write it out. People just seem to assume that it's perfectly natural that there are lots and lots of different types of dinosaurs. But for some reason, when it comes to monkeys and apes, some people don't expect this same type of diversity. ABOVE SOURCE: Rates of Dinosaur Body Mass Evolution Indicate 170 Million Years of Sustained Ecological Innovation on the Avian Stem Lineage If you want to get more technical about it, it comes down to niche partitioning. Different organisms specialize in different diets and ecological niches. In the diagram below, you can see how different antelope species all specialize in slightly different niches, leading to the diversity among those species. It wouldn't do any good, for example, for a reedbuck to 'try' to evolve to become more like a nyala. The reedbuck already has a niche where it survives and that it's well adapted to, while the nyala are already well adapted to their niche. Any reedbuck that tried to push into the Nyala's niche wouldn't be able to compete. ABOVE: Niche partitioning slide from a good presentation - follow the link below to watch the whole thing SOURCE: Niche Partitioning It's the same way with monkeys and apes. If you go far enough back, there is a single common ancestor that we all evolved from. But evolution followed the same pattern in primates as in any other group – splitting and diversifying to take advantage of various different ecological niches. ABOVE: Primate family tree SOURCE: Nelson, Gilbert, Wong, Miller, Price (2012) Every monkey and ape still alive is just as evolved as any other. We just took different evolutionary paths to take advantage of different niches.

If tiktaalik evolved into acanthostega, why are there no intermediary forms? Why are there no intermediary forms between any two creatures that one evolved from? This reminds me of an old joke. A creationist complains to a scientist about a gap in the fossil record between an ancient animal and a modern one. The scientist gets lucky and finds a transitional form intermediate between the two. But the creationist just replies, 'Well now you've made the problem even worse. Instead of only one gap, now you have two.' Tiktaalik was only discovered in 2004. At the time, it was heralded as a near-perfect transitional form between fish like Panderichthyes and Eushthenopteron and early tetrapods like Acanthostega and Ichthyostega, and even acquired the nickname of being a 'fishibian'. It seems it didn't take long for creationists to now see two gaps instead of just one. But to actually answer the question, the reason is because fossils are quite rare. When most organisms die, their remains are completely consumed by scavengers and decomposers. It takes a very unique and unlikely set of circumstances to preserve their remains and go through the fossilization process. And then it takes another fortuitous set of circumstances for those fossils to be exposed through erosion, and then found before erosion carries on further and destroys them completely. The fossils we've found only represent a small subset of all the life that has ever existed on this planet. Just for perspective, consider the non-bird dinosaurs. We've only found something like 700 – 1000 non-bird dinosaurs species from their entire 165 million year history. In comparison, there are 6500 named mammal species just in the present, not counting unnamed living species, or the many, many species that have existed in the past and are now extinct. So we know that the actual number of dinosaur species over that entire 165 million year history must have been orders of magnitude higher than the mere 1000 species we've found so far. And it's the same for other groups of organisms. We know that the fossil record is largely incomplete, especially the fossils we've found so far. Some transitions are extremely well documented (like older apes to modern humans). Some remain pretty much entirely undiscovered (like non-flying animals to pterosaurs). But most fall somewhere in between (like fish to tetrapods). As researchers make more and more discoveries, they continue to fill in the gaps in our understanding. And for the time being, at least, this process shows no signs of slowing down. But even though we'll probably never know all of the details, everything we have found points squarely to natural evolutionary processes. Just as a side note, given how incomplete the fossil record is, it's very unlikely that we've found direct ancestor to descendant relationships in most cases. The transitional forms are more like cousins of the actual ancestors. In some cases, we know that certain fossils can't be ancestors because of the timeframes, but that instead they've preserved certain ancestral conditions.

Is it true that the shooter at Trump's rally was a registered Republican with conservative beliefs and a gun enthusiast? Why are conservatives blaming the left for this incident? There's simply not much to go on to identify his political leanings at this point. Back in 2021, when he was 17, he made a $15 donation to a progressive organization, ActBlue. And yes, despite online rumors, it most likely really was him. When he was old enough to vote, he registered as a Republican. This could mean he legitimately was a Republican. But given that Pennsylvania has a closed primary, this could also mean he wanted to participate in the Republican primary rather than the Democratic primary. As a liberal living in Texas with an open primary, I've voted in the Republican primary before, since I figured it was my only realistic option of trying to influence the governor's race (the Republican I preferred still lost). He seemed to like guns, trying out for his school's shooting team and being a member of a local gun range. At the time of the shooting, he was wearing a t-shirt for a gun enthusiast YouTube channel. But while enthusiasm for guns does skew a bit towards conservative political leanings, it's not at all a sure thing. I like taking my own pistol to the range, for example, and I know plenty of other liberals and Democrats who own and shoot guns. (I'll add that I've seen a few gun enthusiasts trying to use a No True Scotsman argument, claiming that a true gun enthusiast wouldn't have missed this shot, would have used a different rifle, etc. But you don't have to be an expert marksman to merely like guns and like going shooting.) In interviews with former classmates, one student who took an American history course with him stated that he "definitely was conservative", and went on to add about a mock debate that, "The majority of the class were on the liberal side, but Tom, no matter what, always stood his ground on the conservative side." But there's any number of reasons to take this hearsay with a grain of salt (the classmate could have been talking big just to get attention; he might not have known the shooter as well as he claimed, the shooter might have just enjoyed arguing, etc.) I'd also point out that people's political motivations can be quite fluid around that age. Whatever he believed at 17 might not be the same as at 18 or 20. And finally, as I've seen many others point out, we don't even know if his motivation was political. The guy who tried to assassinate Reagan did it to try to get the attention of a movie star. At this point, anybody claiming to know definitively one way or the other which way the shooter leaned politically is not looking at the evidence objectively. And it's an even bigger stretch to try to definitively claim that politics were his main motivation. Investigators are doing their best to figure out his motives. So until then, or until more public evidence comes to light, let's try to keep our speculations grounded in what's actually known. Update 2024–07–22: While it’s still a bit early to say anything definitive about the shooter, the emerging picture seems to be that he was looking for notoriety by shooting somebody famous, not any particular political leanings. In addition to Trump, he’d been searching online for Biden and other prominent political figures. The proximity of the Trump rally to his hometown seems like it might have been the biggest motivator in him choosing Trump over any of the other people he’d been considering.

How did the dinosaurs evolve into chickens? Let's start with the big dinosaur family tree for some perspective: ABOVE SOURCE: Dinosaur classification - Wikipedia As you can see, birds are a type of theropod dinosaur. They first evolved some time around the middle to late Jurassic. They went through a major bottle neck at the end of the Cretaceous in the mass extinction that wiped out nearly all of the dinosaurs, but a handful of birds managed to survive and carry on the lineage. As far as how birds in particular evolved from non-flying dinosaurs, let's start with a high level diagram from Thomas Holtz's online lecture notes: ABOVE SOURCE: Mesozoic Birds and the Origin of Flight This shows in general the order of appearance of the various characteristics that we now regard as 'birdlike'. It starts way back before even dinosaurs with the hinge-like ankle, and includes traits that evolved over generations, through non-flying dinosaurs, and eventually resulting in modern birds (I intentionally didn't say 'culminating', because who knows what's in store for bird evolution in the future.) Here's another diagram from Dr. Holtz. This one focuses a bit tighter on the emergence of birds. They evolved out of the specific theropods known as eumaniraptora. ABOVE SOURCE: Rise of the Birds If you loosely count all Avialae as birds, their closest cousins were the deinonychosaurs, which looked an awful lot like birds, but couldn't fly. Between these two diagrams, they illustrate that many traits that we now associate with birds evolved for ground-based animals, and so must have served purposes that had nothing to do with flight. This includes feathers. More primitive down-like feathers were probably just for insulation, while more complex feathers might have evolved for display. Deinonychosaurs even had 'wing' feathers, despite their arms not being wings, so even these feathers had some other purpose – perhaps as a way to flap to help boost their running abilities, or maybe as a way to help them 'parachute' from long drops, or maybe something else. But obviously, with such feathers evolving before birds, flight couldn't have been their original purpose. I don't know as much about chicken evolution in particular. But chickens are domesticated animals, and their wild ancestors were red junglefowl. This is a species of bird that spends a lot of its time foraging on the ground, but which can still fly when the need arises. ABOVE SOURCE: Reddit ABOVE SOURCE: Red Junglefowl in flight - Bird Ecology Study Group Jungle fowl are part of a larger group that includes pheasants, partridges, turkeys, and peacocks. Here's a larger family tree of birds to show where they fit in (the Galliformes): ABOVE SOURCE: Evolutionary Radiation of Birds So that's the quick story. A lot of 'bird like' traits had already evolved in non-flying dinosaurs, such as feathers, being warm blooded, their air sac respiratory system, etc. Then, one particular branch of dinosaurs, the birds, evolved the ability to fly, and began diversifying from there. There was a major bottleneck when most species of birds were wiped out at the end of the Cretaceous, which wiped out a lot of the then existing variation (like many birds still having teeth), but the survivors went on to diversify into all the birds we have today, including chickens. What are the scientific odds of human existence? What conditions are necessary for life to exist? That's a very interesting question (the first one). The late Stephen Jay Gould came up with a thought experiment of 'rewinding' the history of life and starting over. Would you get the same results? How much of evolution is driven by randomness and chance, how much is driven by contingency, and how much is driven by more general principles? Here's how Gould himself put it: Suppose that ten of a hundred designs will survive and diversify. If the ten survivors are predictable by superiority of anatomy (Interpretation 1), then they will win each time – and Burgess eliminations do not challenge our comforting view of life. But if the ten survivors are protégés of Lady Luck or fortunate beneficiaries of odd historical contingencies (Interpretation 2), then each replay of the tape will yield a different set of survivors and a radically different history. And if you recall from high-school algebra how to calculate permutations and combinations, you will realize that the total number of combinations for 10 items from a pool of 100 yields more than 17 trillion potential outcomes. There's one particular experiment that comes as close as I can think of to replaying the tape of life, in the small scale, at least*. Back in 1988, Richard Lenski started out with one strain of E. coli, and split it into 12 different populations. He grew each population in identical conditions (well, as close to identical as experimentally possible) which were actually somewhat harsh for E. coli. He used a particular growth medium named DM25, which has a limited amount of glucose that the E. coli need to feed on. Lenski wanted to see how the E. coli would evolve due to this limited food supply. Every day, he would transfer 1% of the previous day's populations to new flasks with a fresh supply of DM25, periodically freezing samples to maintain as a kind of 'fossil record', and also periodically measuring attributes of the populations to see how they were evolving. The experiment is still ongoing today, making it one of the longest running (and supremely well documented) evolutionary experiments. Here's how one particular trait evolved in each of these populations, cell size: ABOVE SOURCE: E. coli long-term evolution experiment - Wikipedia While there's a general trend of increasing cell size in all 12 populations, they didn't all follow the exact same trend. In fact, the largest lineage evolved to be nearly twice as big as the smallest lineage. One particular adaptation was so rare that it only occurred in one of Lenski's populations.* The DM25 growth medium also happened to contain a large amount of citrate, which E. coli usually can't digest in anaerobic conditions, but which was included in the DM25 formulation way back when it was first developed for antibiotic experiments because it improved the efficiency of penicillin. Well, in this single lineage of Lenski's twelve E. coli populations, they did evolve the ability to digest citrate in anaerobic conditions. This adaptation is so profound for E. coli that some have proposed it actually represents a new species. So, starting from identical genetics, and subjecting populations to as identical of conditions as experimentally possible, each of the 12 populations took their own different evolutionary paths, from cell size, to the ability to digest citrate, to other traits I didn't mention here. There wasn't simply one optimum set of adaptations that natural selection drove towards in each population. This really does seem to indicate that chance† and contingency are major factors in the evolution of populations. And Lenski's experiment only had 12 isolated populations. What if he'd had 100? Would there be 100 unique strains by now? What about 1000? Or a million? Or to put it into the terminology of this question, what are the scientific odds of any particular strain of E. coli evolving in any particular flask? Based on Lenski's experiment, we can say it's no greater than 1 out of 12, but the reality could be a much, much smaller probability. So, let that play out in every population that's ever existed, and it seems that every particular species has a very low probability of existing‡. That goes for everything from ocelots to dandelions to Humboldt's squid to portabella mushrooms. And yes, it goes for us humans, as well. To add one more thing, it does seem like some body plans or adaptations are more common than others, implying that there are general principles that drive these adaptations. Levers to propel an organism on the seafloor or land, aka legs, have evolved in animals as diverse as insects, tetrapods, and starfish. Free swimming organisms evolved streamlined hydrodynamic bodies. Flying animals evolve wings. Etc. But other adaptations appear to be quite rare, like Lenski's citrate digesting E. coli. If elephants were to go extinct, I'm not sure we'd ever see another animal with that kind of trunk. And I can only hope that when aye-ayes go extinct, that particular combination of nightmare fuel never reappears. I rather suspect that we humans are kind of like elephants in that respect. You simply don't see many other animals similar to us outside our closest evolutionary cousins. We have a weird combination of an upright bipedal posture, complex social groups, extremely high intelligence with a penchant for technology combined with hands that are really good at manipulating our environments to effect that technology, along with several other unique characteristics. So, outside the general principle of all particular species being highly improbable, I'd say that even a species along the lines of us humans is highly improbable. Play the tape of life 1000 times, and while you might get lots of critters superficially resembling a crab, you might not get another elephant or another human. While I'm not sure anybody can give the precise odds, I think it's safe to say that the odds of human existence were quite low. So much of evolution is driven by chance and contingency, and we seem to be a rather odd combination of traits on top of that. That's all the more reason we need to get our acts together and make sure we don't screw up our planet (whether through things like climate change or good old fashioned global thermonuclear war). Because if we do go extinct, the odds are decent that nothing with our ability for science and understanding will ever evolve on this planet, again. *Both of these paragraphs are mostly copied from a previous answer of mine: †Chance could be things like Genetic drift or even the raw material of random mutation. ‡Don't confuse low probabilities of a particular species with low probabilities of life in general. A common analogy is shuffling a deck of cards. With 52 unique cards, the odds of any particular order for an entire deck is 1 in 10^68, an astronomically tiny probability. But, you're essentially guaranteed some order of 52 cards. That's the way it is with evolution and species – the odds of any particular species may be infinitesimally small, but the evolution of species in general is pretty much guaranteed. Argh. Why is the Francesinha the world's best sandwich? This question contains a fallacy, and so it can’t be answered as asked. Now, I’d never heard of the Francesinha before coming across this question. Sandwiches are meant to be eaten with your hands. That’s kind of the whole point from the very earliest times when the Earl of Sandwich invented them. If you need a knife and a fork to eat a food, that’s not a sandwich. I mean, you could put your bacon in between your French toast, but that wouldn’t make it a sandwich. So however good a Francesinha might taste, it can’t take the title for world’s best sandwich*. So what is the best sandwich? Man, there are just way too many choices to narrow it down to one. You’ve got everything from hoagies to BLTs to Reubens to club sandwiches to Bánh mì to panini to tortas to cheesesteaks to Primanti’s and on and on and on. Why is the left so adamant in their denial that COVID-19 came from the Wuhan virology lab? It's like a chocolate flood in Hershey, Pennsylvania. Might it be from the candy factory? Let's start off with the likelihood of where the pandemic originated before getting into the politics. First, although I realize that appeals to authority aren't a strictly logical argument, expert opinion is still a very useful heuristic. These are folks who have in depth knowledge and expertise on a topic, and much more likely to have a well informed opinion than a random stranger on the Internet. And the natural animal origin (zoonotic origin if you want to get technical) is the clear consensus. That's not to say that a lab leak is impossible. It just seems much less likely at this point, especially among the folks who have devoted their careers to studying such things. ABOVE: Results of a survey of 168 virologists, infectious disease epidemiologists, and other scientists SOURCE: The Origin and Implications of the COVID-19 Pandemic: An Expert Survey | Global Catastrophic Risk Institute (click through to the PDF report) I also came across a very informative debate about the issue. If you have a half hour or so, I'd really recommend reading the whole thing: I think the two pieces of evidence that I found the most convincing had to do with the original cases. They were centered around the wet market in Wuhan, not the Wuhan Institute of Virology: ABOVE SOURCE: Practically-A-Book Review: Rootclaim $100,000 Lab Leak Debate And even more specifically, the cases within the market were centered around a racoon dog vendor, an animal which is a known carrier of COVID-19: ABOVE SOURCE: Practically-A-Book Review: Rootclaim $100,000 Lab Leak Debate In fact, two years before the pandemic, a scientist who was visiting that very same market took a picture of the conditions of the racoon dogs, because he was told even back then that "This is the kind of place that has the ingredients for cross-species transmission of dangerous pathogens." ABOVE: Conditions of racoon dogs and birds in the wet market back in 2014 SOURCE: NPR IMAGE CREDIT: Eddie Holmes As that debate I linked to put it: People say it would be a surprising coincidence if a zoonotic coronavirus pandemic just so happened to start in a city with a big coronavirus research lab, and this is true. But it would be an even more surprising coincidence if a lab-leak coronavirus pandemic just so happened to first get detected at a raccoon-dog stall in a wet market! The other piece of evidence concerning the first cases has to do with the two separate early lineages of COVID-19, Lineage A and Lineage B. Lineage B is the one centered specifically in the wet market. But even Lineage A was first found in a neighborhood nearby the market. Quoting that debate once more: Again, it would be a bizarre coincidence if a lab leak pandemic was first detected at a wet market. But it would be an even more bizarre coincidence if a lab leak pandemic separated into two strains, and both were first detected at a wet market! Another strong piece of evidence is that COVID-19 seems most likely to have evolved from a related coronavirus, BANAL-52. But BANAL-52 wasn't discovered until after the pandemic, once interest in the origins of COVID-19 had spiked and people were trying very hard to determine where it came from. It's hard to study a virus in a lab that you haven't discovered yet. Of course, there's plenty more detail to it than that. Like I already said, I'd highly recommend reading that debate I already linked to. Here's another good, somewhat shorter article from a few years ago, and a podcast that I've heard is good (but I prefer reading to listening to podcasts, so I haven't listened to it myself): [ETA - Here’s another good link I just ran across:] None of this is to say that the natural origin is 100% likely, or that the lab leak has a 0% probability. But it certainly does seem like the natural origin is the more likely explanation. Okay, so what about the political aspect of it? I'd like to say that it's because 'my' side of the aisle is always rational and evidence based, and so they're just following the science. And there's certainly a troubling strain of anti-intellectualism and anti-science infecting the Republican party right now, as I explained in a previous answer (Some worry that the United States is in an unusually anti-intellectual period right now. Is this really the case? Haven't societies always been composed mostly of people who are rather unthinking and just want "bread and circuses"?). But as I also noted in that answer: I'm a bit cynical about the Democratic support of science. While I'd love for it to be authentic, I suspect it's mostly virtue signaling in opposition to the Republican distrust of science. But at least lip service in support of science is still better than organized opposition. In other words, I suspect many folks on the left are so adamant in their support of the natural origin of COVID-19 not because they understand the science, but because so many people on the right seem to support the lab leak hypothesis, and so this issue, like so many others, has become divided along party lines, and a way to advertise your allegiance to your own tribe. But just to return briefly to the main point of this answer – the evidence really does point to a natural origin of COVID-19 as being the most likely explanation. Maybe not 100% certain, but more certain than a lab leak.

How was the 2024 solar eclipse? Was there much of a panic/emergency as the USA prepared for or just a fizzle? The thing about preparing for potential emergencies, is that if you do your job well and avoid any problems, then everybody wonders what the fuss was about in the first place. The legitimate concerns around this eclipse (outside the conspiracy theories on Facebook) were mainly centered around so many people coming together in one area – things like traffic jams or strains on the supply chain (particularly food and fuel). Such concerns were based off the prior experiences of the 2017 eclipse. A report on traffic conditions, for example (TR News - Traffic Impacts of the 2017 Solar Eclipse), found that at least 5 million people had traveled to view that eclipse, that nearly all the Interstate highways in the path of totality ended up red on Google Maps immediately after the eclipse, and that some trips that would normally only take 4 hours by car actually took 13 hours in the wake of the eclipse. So, in preparation, some locations pre-emptively declared a state of emergency to be better able to address such concerns, or to be able to mobilize the National Guard for extra manpower just in case they would be needed, or made sure that highway related positions were all fully manned (e.g. toll booths, rest stops, emergency vehicles, etc.). Traffic did still turn out pretty bad in some places (there’s only so much you can do without changing the infrastructure), but I haven't heard of any major incidents or problems. So were officials over-prepared? Or did they just do a good job and help curtail any problems before they happened?

Is baldness a survival benefit, in the sense of Darwin's evolutionary theory of "The Survival of the Fittest"? How is baldness adventagous for survival? Meh. Who knows? Stephen J. Gould and Richard C. Lewontin wrote a seminal article cautioning against ultra-adaptationist thinking all the way back in 1979: Here's a good excerpt from the paper: We fault the adaptationist programme for its failure to distinguish current utility from reasons for origin (male tyrannosaurs may have used their diminutive front legs to titillate female partners, but this will not explain why they got so small); for its unwillingness to consider alternatives to adaptive stories; for its reliance upon plausibility alone as a criterion for accepting speculative tales; and for its failure to consider adequately such competing themes as random fixation of alleles, production of non-adaptive structures by developmental correlation with selected features (allometry, pleiotropy, material compensation, mechanically forced correlation), the separability of adaptation and selection, multiple adaptive peaks, and current utility as an epiphenomenon of non-adaptive structures. The moral is, before you try to invent just-so stories about the evolutionary advantage of a trait, you have to demonstrate that it was positively selected for in the first place. It might very well just be the result of random drift, with no real effect on fitness. A different, more recent, article by Larry Moran, On the importance of random genetic drift in modern evolutionary theory, contained these examples: Take a favorite example of Richard Lewontin who points to the fact that the African rhinoceros has two horns while the Indian rino has only one? Is this an example of natural selection? Are two horns better than one in Africa or is the null hypothesis just as likely? What about the difference between red pine, with two needles per cluster, and white pine, with five? Are those adaptations or are they just due to neutral alleles that have become fixed in the two species? Is it possible that the genes that lead to baldness have some benefit? Sure. Maybe baldness itself is attractive to some women and so affected by sexual selection. Maybe the genes that lead to baldness have other effects that are beneficial. But this type of speculation is turning into the just-so stories that Gould and Lewontin warned against. Not every feature that we've evolved was necessarily down to natural selection. Random chance plays its role, as well. I did find one fairly reasonable article that described a study showing that bald-headed men are "consistently rated as more intelligent, influential, knowledgeable, well-educated, high social status, honest and helpful – traits collectively known as social maturity." So maybe there is something to that. But it's still pretty speculative at this point.

What is the best religious factual book you read so I can buy it and read it? For Christianity and Judaism, out of the books I've read, at least, there are plenty I could recommend. But there's one in particular that I think should be in the everybody’s collection as a base reference – the New Oxford Annotated Bible*. It has very good essays as introductory material to each individual book, as well as each larger collection of books (e.g. The Pentateuch, the Historical Books, etc.). The essays were written by serious Biblical scholars, some religious themselves, some not, and hence do their best to present well backed up scholarly consensus not biased by either religious or anti-religious motivations. They explain things such as the origins and authorship of each book from a scholarly perspective (as opposed to the traditional authorships, e.g. the Documentary hypothesis), themes, styles, etc. Throughout each book, it has extensive footnotes to explain in more detail these subjects, translation issues, historical background, etc. At the end of the entire book, it has another couple hundred pages of supporting materials, including more essays, a glossary, concordance information, an index, and maps. To give an idea, here's an example spread from Isaiah. Note how much information is provided in the footnotes below the Biblical text: ABOVE SOURCE: New Oxford Annotated Bible NRSV 5th Edition Beyond that, the translation used is the New Revised Standard Version (NRSV), which is one that seems to be very well respected among the Biblical scholars I've read, such as Bart Ehrman, the late Hector Avalos, and the late Bruce Metzger. In contrast to another well known translation, the New Internation Version, the translators of the NRSV really do seem to have tried their best to present the message that the original writers meant, rather than letting their modern day religious views bias their efforts. Here's a bit more info on the topic of translations, if you're interested: Now, given that the essays and footnotes are written by Biblical scholars, you won't get something like a comparison of Genesis to a scientific understanding of the history of our universe. But you will get explanations from critical analysis with a bit of archaeological discussion to explain how we know that those stories are myths and not literal history. (And just to be clear, yes, many religious folks accept the moral lessons of the Bible without believing that the stories are literally true.) Of course, reading the entire thing is a project. It's over 2000 pages long, with a small font size to boot. But it gives a good understanding of the factual vs. legendary/mythical aspects of the Bible, and how Biblical scholars were able to make those distinctions. And since the essays and footnotes are written by Biblical scholars, you know you're getting mainstream scholarly consensus, not polemics. *To be fair, I've also heard that the Harper Collins Study Bible is also very good (and there are likely more), but the New Oxford Annotated Bible is the one that seemed most recommended back when I was looking for a study Bible, so it's the one I went with.

Why did it take until the 1900s before flying was invented, when the kite was invented in the 5th century? Engines. Although it might seem primitive by today's standards, here's the engine that powered the Wright Brothers' first plane, designed and built by their mechanic, Charlie Taylor. ABOVE SOURCE: 1903 Wright Engine That engine weighed 180 lbs and put out 12 horsepower. Again, that might not seem like much compared to the hugely powerful engines we have today, but horsepower really is roughly equivalent to what a horse can manage continuously (though they can go much higher for short bursts of a few seconds), so that 180 lb engine is basically doing the work of 12 horses. That's a lot. Steam engines probably could have gotten there. In fact, some of the earliest experiments with unmanned flying machines did use steam engines. And more modern steam engines have had decent power to weight ratios. ABOVE: The steam powered, unmanned Aerodrome No. 5 in flight in 1896. SOURCE: This Odd Early Flying Machine Made History but Didn't Have the Right Stuff Spruce and fabric are old technologies, so people could have built the frames and wings of aircraft for millennia. But prior to steam engines and internal combustion engines, people simply didn't have a power source with enough power at a light enough weight to enable flying machines.

The Grimm brothers collected a particular story that touches on this, The Shepherd Boy. Just imagine living long enough to see that mountain get worn down. And then again. And again. And again, never ending. Could you really maintain a joie de vivre for eternity? Or would boredom or ennui eventually settle in? And depending on the scenario, imagine just how horrible it would be if you were the only immortal being. What makes Google Maps superior to Apple Maps? One reason – north up maps. Maybe I'm just old fashioned from the old days of using paper maps*. But I really, really, really prefer maps to always be oriented as north up when I'm driving. I know it might not be the most intuitive when you need to make split second decisions. But in the long run, it gives you a much better perspective and sense of orientation. Especially when you're in an area where you might be spending some time and not just driving through once, it really helps you learn the area. I have a sense of the actual cardinal direction I'm heading, not just 'straight ahead'. I can see where neighborhoods lie in relation to each other. I can build up a mental map that corresponds to the map I see on the screen. In contrast, the maps that are constantly rotating to align with your direction of travel just completely destroy that sense of awareness and perspective. When I spent a few months in El Paso a couple years ago, I learned my way around much quicker thanks to Google Maps always keeping the map with north up. Otherwise, despite an ignominious beginning**, Apple Maps has grown into a decent app. It even seems to do better than Google Maps at some things, like telling you which lane to be in, and giving you more than one next step at a time. But until Apple decides to put in an option for users to keep the map oriented as north up even in guidance mode, I'm simply not going to use it. *I remember back when I was a kid, on road trip vacations, or when we first moved from Pennsylvania to Maryland, and I'd sit in the back seat of the car following along on a map to see where we were. Maybe it was all those years of practice that helps me follow along on north up maps, when so many other folks I know seem to get confused by it. **If you look at the other answers to this question, the ones trashing Apple Maps tend to be several years old. It really is a decent app, now, minus that one, monumental shortcoming.

Why do people have a problem with Christianity so much? Or is it because they think it might/could be the true religion? As an atheist, I don't think any religions are true. But living in the U.S., our country is so saturated with Christianity that Christianity is the religion that affects me by far the most. Here, for example, are the results from a fairly recent poll on the religious makeup in the U.S.: ABOVE SOURCE: The Largest Survey Ever Conducted of American Religious and Denominational Identity: 14 Major Findings from a Landmark Study Note that all the blue and green slices are Christians. Purple and grey are unaffiliated or people who didn't respond. Only those small orange slices are non-Christian religions (and arguably, Jehovah's Witnesses should have been included with the Christians instead). None of those other religions make up a large enough percentage of the population to have much influence. Anecdotally, I've never had a Buddhist come knocking on my door to preach their scriptures. I've never found Muslim tracts hidden in books at the bookstore. I haven't seen Hindus shouting with a megaphone on a street corner when I was just trying to get into the Stars game. But I've experienced all of those, and more, from Christians. And that's not even getting into the political influence of those Christians. Notice how nearly a quarter of those folks in the above graph were Unaffiliated, and it's actually closer to 30% in more recent surveys (How U.S. religious composition has changed in recent decades). But do you know what the Congress and Senate look like? ABOVE SOURCE: Faith on the Hill In the House, nobody specifically identified as unaffiliated, atheist, or agnostic. Though a whopping 1 person did identify as Humanist, and 3.7% responded with "Don't know/Refused to answer". In the Senate, there was 1 senator who identified as unaffiliated, and a further 4 who went with the "Don't know/Refused to answer". So in a nation where around 30% of the population is religiously unaffiliated, and only around 2/3 are Christians, 88% of House members are Christian, while 85% of Senators are. Now, I know that plenty of Christians are perfectly capable of separating their religious beliefs from secular concerns, and do respect the First Amendment's separation of church and state, and that it's not all Christians trying to enforce religiously based laws. But still, for those of us who aren't Christians, it would be nice if our government representatives were a little more representative. Basically, we have 'so much' of a problem with Christianity, because that's the religion that actually causes us problems. I don't think any of the other religions are right*, either, but they simply don't have much influence in the U.S. *Okay, technically, not all religions spend much effort on the supernatural, and are more about philosophies, e.g. Unitarian Universalists. So they're not necessarily wrong in the same way as religions which make objective claims about reality.

What hasn't natural selection eliminated criminals and selfishness? Do we need a few more billion years? While evolution is a mindless process without any conscious intent, sometimes anthropomorphizing can help to explain things. And in that sense, the 'goal' of evolution is to produce more offspring. And in a social animal like us, that sets up conflicting imperatives. Depending on the conditions and the niche, social groups and cooperation can offer animals synergistic benefits greater than the sum of the individuals. If you've ever tried working on DIY projects by yourself, you've probably found times where two people working together can get the job done in less than half the time of one person working alone. So, for example, if I help my neighbor build a shed, and then he helps me build mine, we'll get two sheds built in less time than it would have taken either of us to try to build our own. It's a win-win. So, you see various levels of social cooperation in all types of packs, herds, tribes, troops, pods, etc., with ants and bees being some of the most extreme examples. Individuals living in such social environments need social instincts, not just to make the group successful, but so that they're accepted into the group so that they can take advantage of the group benefits for themselves. If I was the cantakerous neighbor that nobody liked, I'd never get anybody to help me on projects. But, there are also conflicting instincts to not be too selfless to the group, lest they sacrifice their own reproductive success. I don't want to go around only helping out neighbors, but never get around to my own projects. Similarly, all members of the group have an interest in identifying and punishing freeloaders and cheats, since they would drag down the success of the group as a whole, and conversely, individuals will have an interest in not being identified as cheats, themselves, to avoid punishment. So, social animals evolve a whole range of complex and sometimes conflicting impulses to maximize their success in such settings. Even actions that go against their own short term self interest may be important in maintaining long term acceptance within the group. I'll give up my own time to help my neighbor move with no expectation of reward other than the obligatory pizza and beer, but it cements my standing in the community as a 'good guy'. Of course, most of us aren't so Machiavellian and calculating in our own behavior, but, anthropomorphizing a bit more, natural selection was. And so, we've evolved all these instincts for noble and selfish impulses. As long as our species survives and we continue to live in these types of social groups, selfishness will unfortunately persist alongside our more noble impulses. It's the way natural selection ensures that we take care of propagating our own genes. We have an entire fossil record of organisms living throughout all those various periods, which points almost indisputably to evolution and common descent. We have comparative anatomy, comparative genetics, biogeography, and countless other patterns that all seem to point towards evolution and common descent. We have observed examples, in the lab and in the wild, of natural selection, new anatomical features, speciation, etc., that all point to evolution occurring right now in the present day. If all this is a trick of Satan, just exactly which character in Christian mythology is supposed to be the real God? Do pro-choice people at least think we should reduce the number of abortions? That's a weird question. It's about like asking if we should reduce the number of bypass surgeries for clogged arteries. On the one hand, as the old saying goes, an ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure. It would be great if we could get people to live healthier lifestyles to avoid clogged arteries and the need for bypass surgeries in the first place. But as long as people do have clogged arteries, I very much want bypass surgery to be available. I don't want to reduce the number of bypass surgeries if the need still remains. And it still remains a fact of life that clogged arteries will happen regardless, so some amount of bypass surgeries will always be necessary. It's similar for abortion. It would be great if everybody had comprehensive sex education and easily available contraception and birth control to reduce the number of accidental pregnancies. And it would be great to have generally good living conditions for all families, easily affordable and accesible prenatal care, or at least adequate social safety nets, so that nobody was worried about having the means to raise a child with a good quality of life and opportunities. And it would be really great if there were no more rapes, developmental abnormalities, or other complications with pregnancies. So of course it would be nice to reduce all the reasons for abortions in the first place. But I don't want to reduce access to abortions while the need remains. And it's still a fact of life that some amount of abortions will always be necessary, because we never will fully eliminate all those reasons. So yes, like with any other healthcare issue, it would be best to reduce the causes that lead to needing medical intervention. But as long as the need's still there, you still provide the healthcare. And it's just a weird way to phrase a question, asking if we want to reduce a specific medical procedure, rather than addressing the causes that lead to that procedure.

If you see an iPhone in the dessert, you'd say someone created it. Why can't the same be said for humans? I've gotta admit – although I've come across Paley's watchmaker analogy plenty of times, thinking about it just now in terms of an iPhone really drove home just how silly of an argument it is. We know exactly how iPhones are made. We can go visit the factories where they're built, or the engineering offices where they're designed. There's a direct trail of evidence to understanding that they're human artifacts. ABOVE SOURCE: Inside Apple's iPhone Factory We also know how people get 'made' (sorry, but I can't include a picture of that one on a family site). There are no factories or engineers involved (well, outside of engineers having kids the old fashioned way). If I come across a human in a desert, I would suspect that they were conceived, born, and raised in the natural way, not that they were some sort of artificial creation. If you want to argue that people are some sort of engineered beings, show the evidence of the factories and designers the same way we can for an iPhone. What's more, beyond the way that individual people are conceived, we have plenty of evidence for evolution for the origin of our species as a whole. We know the mechanisms and patterns. We understand many of the genetic processes. We've found fossils showing the evolution of humans from prior ape species (and plenty of other evolutionary histories besides just us people, but I'm sticking to the topic of the question). ABOVE SOURCE: Julian Norris's answer to What is the most complete visual human evolution chart available? So if you're going to try to argue that humans are somehow engineered or designed, not only do you need to find evidence of the factories and the designers, you have to also account for all the evidence we have that currently seems to point exclusively to evolution. Were all those older hominids previous models? Did the designer(s) release upgrades every few millennia? Assuming the designer(s) designed other organisms besides just us people, why did they seem to self-impose limitations of a nested hierarchy, never taking good design improvements (like feathers or mammary glands) and using them in a different group? It would be like when GM first introduced airbags in the Oldsmobile Toronado, and that all subsequent installations of airbags would be limited to other Oldsmobiles, and never carried over to other products in GM's portfolio, and never adopted by other designers at other automakers. Basically, iPhones and biological beings are completely different things. It just seems silly to try to compare the design and manufacture of iPhones to people.

At what point will bees evolve to sting without dying? This would surely improve their survival, no? Honeybees current trait of dying when they sting mammals already is the more evolved form. Bees are a part of a larger suborder known as Apocrita, which also contains wasps and ants, and stingers are common throughout this group. The stingers evolved from ovipositors (a fancy word meaning basically 'egg depositor'), and as such, only females have stingers. In most of the insects in this group, including solitary bees, the stingers are not barbed, and don't tear away from the insect while stinging. That is the ancestral condition, and it allows such individuals to sting without dying themselves (which is especially important for the solitary species). But in bees that developed to live in hives, they evolved the specialization of a barbed stinger that can become stuck in the skin of mammals, and then tear away from the abdomen of the bee, leaving behind the venom sack and pumping organs. This maximizes the dose of venom that can be delivered, since merely brushing the bee away still leaves all that venom injecting 'equipment', which can continue pumping venom until it's all been injected. ABOVE SOURCE: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/312574312_Immunology_of_Bee_Venom The reason this makes sense in honeybees is because of their communal organization. Bee hives are often described as 'superorganisms'. The hive itself acts as the unit of reproduction. More specifically, only queens lay eggs, not workers (in the honeybee species with queens – remember that many bee species are solitary, and some only form loose colonies, not the highly organized hives). If the death of a worker does enough to protect the hive as a whole, then it's worth the loss of that individual. It's also worth noting that queens don't have barbed stingers, since the loss of a queen would be a huge loss to the hive. (Queens aren't completely irreplaceable. A new larvae can be raised to become a new queen, but that's still a big loss in egg laying output before the new queen has developed, which is much more impactful than the loss of a single worker.) The other thing to point out is that even in honeybees, when stinging other insects, the barbed stingers usually don't become stuck. The bee can sting an insect once, then move on. And of course, this makes sense, since it won't take nearly as much venom to incapacitate a small insect as it would take to drive off a much larger mammal. The final point is that honeybee workers typically only survive for about 6 weeks during the summer (whereas the queens live for 2 – 5 years). So even if they did somehow survive stinging a mammal, they wouldn't be around that much longer, anyway – certainly not enough time to regrow a new stinger and venom organs. So really, the stinging mechanism of honeybees is already highly derived and optimized for their lifestyles. It's not so much that dying is the goal, but maximizing the amount of venom that can be injected into mammalian threats, and the death of a worker is just a side effect of that. But since the hive itself is the important unit for reproductive success, and workers have such short lifespans to begin with, the death of a few workers is an appropriate tradeoff to maximize venom delivery.

Do atheists actually believe they are monkeys? Do they have an urge to climb trees? Is it sad to only believe in one’s self? Let's take these one at a time: Do atheists actually believe they are monkeys? Meh. It's a semantics issue. I'm definitely an ape. And I'm definitely a primate, and definitely a mammal. And on and on for all the various larger taxonomic groups we're included in. But whether or not you think we're monkeys comes down to whether you think monkeys are a monophyletic, paraphyletic, or polyphyletic group. You can debate it, but it doesn't change the reality of the animals we evolved from. (FWIW, I have come around to thinking monkeys should be monophyletic, and that us apes are just a slightly specialized branch of monkeys.) ABOVE: Aegyptopithecus, which was a close cousin to our ancestors, and thus would have been very similar. SOURCE: Aegyptopithecus (note: the above image itself is valid, but Reptile Evolution is a bit of a dubious site - David Peters started off as a decent paleoartist, but kind of went off the deep end a couple decades back) Do they have an urge to climb trees? Yes. Don't you? I climbed trees all the time as a kid, and now that I'm an adult, it's only decorum (and aging joints) that keeps me from climbing them more often. But I still do climb trees from time to time. And when I got some scaffolding to do some work around the house, I told my wife it was like having a grown up jungle gym, and that it gave me an excuse to climb on it for 'work' instead of just playing around. Is it sad to only believe in one’s self? What does that have to do with atheism? I have eyes. I can see an entire world full of other people, animals, plants, etc. There's very much just here on Earth to believe in besides myself. And that's before you start looking at pictures of space, and the untold number of entire galaxies besides our own.

Why does my keyboard have a caps lock key? It must have some purpose, right? This is a good question. Is there really a need for a caps lock key on modern keyboards? How many times do most people use it intentionally, vs. eNDING UP WITH SENTENCES UNINTENTIONALLY WRITTEN IN ALL CAPS? The obvious function is that it lets you write in all caps, LIKE THIS, without having to hold down the shift key. This stems from old, mechanical typewriters, where the shift key actually did mechanically shift the typing mechanism to switch between lower case and upper case letters, which required a decent amount of force on the key. So, for prolonged all caps typing, a shift-lock locked the mechanism in the shifted position, easing the load on your pinky fingers. But shift-lock shifted all the keys, including the symbols on numbers, so a slightly later innovation was caps-lock that only shifted the letters, not the entire keyboard. Once electric typewriters, word processors, and early computers came around, the effort to hold down shift wasn’t nearly so hard, but it was still nice to have a caps-lock key. Remember that typewriters and early printers (like Daisy wheels) still didn’t allow for much formatting or different font sizes, so all-caps was still a convenient way to distinguish things like titles and headings. But on modern day computers? Just about any serious project that needs to be in all-caps can be handled by software, and in many cases, it’s even preferable to do it that way. For example, for headings in a paper, you should type them out in normal mixed case, e.g. Heading Example. Then, if you want it in all caps, just change the heading style to all caps, and the word processing software will take care of it for you. But if you decide later to switch back to mixed case, it’s just a quick change of the style rather than re-typing everything. In my own field, technical drawings use all caps as the standard for drawing annotations, but this can also be handled through software settings instead of using caps-lock (e.g. Displaying Annotation Notes in Uppercase). Even typing here on Quora, there are already a basic text formatting options. Adding an all-caps to that would be simple. There may be some niche applications, like programming, where caps-lock still has a bit of use, but I imagine a lot of that’s driven by complacency. Remove the caps-lock key from the keyboard, and programming software would pretty quickly include software features*. The more I think about it, the more I’d like to see the caps-lock key done away with, to free up that space on the keyboard for something more useful. Maybe replace it with a keyboard shortcut to enable all caps (like alt-shift-c), or at least relegate it to a far corner of the keyboard where you’re less likely to hit it by accident. Here’s something related I found doing a bit of googling: *I’m only a novice programmer, with most of my experience in Visual Basic (which just earned me several snorts of derision from the real programmers). But even back in VB 6, I only worried about capitalization when I declared my variables. After that, I typed them in all lower case, and VB would automatically convert them to the capitalization from when they were declared. Not only did it save me the effort of pressing the shift key, it was a nice, quick double check that I typed in the correct variable name (if it didn’t update capitalization, I’d made a typo).
